title: Houthi Missiles Reach Mecca and Medina's Airspace, Kim Jong Un Inaugurates the Yalu Bridge, and Brazil Votes in a Coin-Toss Runoff
subhead: Iran-aligned Houthis claim strikes on three Saudi airports and Saudi oil sites while Riyadh reports intercepts over Islam's two holiest cities. Kim Jong Un crosses into China for the first time in over a year as Pyongyang's ties with Seoul deteriorate. Brazilians choose between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

sections.heading: The Houthis Expand Their Target Set From Saudi Infrastructure to the Holy Cities
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia's civil defence service said on Saturday that the Houthis had fired two ballistic missiles toward Mecca and Medina and warned of falling shrapnel after intercepting them, according to Al Jazeera. Images distributed by the Saudi Press Agency showed a large blackened missile-shaped object that had come down somewhere in the kingdom. The Houthis rejected the account outright, calling it a 'huge lie' and saying their actual targets were three Saudi airports plus oil facilities. The group also struck inside Yemen itself: the internationally recognised government's transport ministry said Aden International Airport was hit by two ballistic missiles, the fourth such attack on the airport this month, and said the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also struck. The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden's naval base.

Casualty and damage claims remain contested in both directions. Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV said Saudi coalition air strikes killed several civilians in Sanaa and Hodeidah, a claim that could not be verified and on which Riyadh has not commented. Yemen's army, meanwhile, said a Houthi missile malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday, killing three people, and described repeated missile malfunctions in recent weeks.

Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi called the attacks 'heinous' and accused the Houthis of a blatant disregard for civilian life. The claim of targeting the holy cities — if believed in Riyadh and the Gulf — sharply raises the political cost of restraint for Saudi leadership, at a moment when Washington has already ordered personnel out of the kingdom and pulled back from Gulf bases.
sections.whyItMatters: Strikes framed as reaching Mecca and Medina convert a proxy war into a legitimacy crisis for the Saudi leadership, and Aden's fourth airport strike this month shows the Houthis can now hit both the Saudi depth and the Yemeni government's seat simultaneously. Every escalation raises the price of the de-escalation Washington is trying to engineer.

sections.heading: Tehran and Washington Trade Blame as Trump Floats a Strike 'as Soon as Sunday'
sections.body:
President Trump said the US is considering a possible attack on Iran as soon as Sunday, telling reporters Washington might have to 'finish the job' or could instead reach a major deal with Tehran, Al Jazeera's live coverage reported on Sunday. On Friday he had said he 'may do another little Epic Fury', using the codename of the US-Israeli war with Iran that began on 28 February.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian blamed Washington for the collapse of interim-agreement talks, calling the Americans 'cowards' who 'messed everything up' in remarks broadcast by Press TV, while insisting both sides should return to the table and conclude a deal. The IRGC warned through the semi-official Fars News Agency that even limited strikes would trigger a response 'several times greater'. Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi said US forces would not be allowed into the Gulf 'under any circumstances and at any time'. Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said Tehran would not 'wait for permission to defend itself'.

CBC reported on Saturday that Israeli and Western analysts expect a third round of direct war after the US midterms, with former Israeli military intelligence official Danny Citrinowicz telling the network that 'a renewed war seems almost inevitable' and that Trump faces 'only bad and worse options'. Both Trump and Netanyahu are heading into elections — Israel votes on Tuesday, the US on 3 November — which gives each an incentive to keep the military option live rather than settle.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between an imminent strike and a signed deal is now measured in hours, and both principals are campaigning. A decision taken under electoral pressure would set the terms of the next phase of the Gulf war with little room for reversal.

sections.heading: Kim Jong Un Crosses the Yalu as Pyongyang Leans Toward Beijing
sections.body:
Kim Jong Un travelled into China on Saturday, crossing the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge to the border city of Dandong, according to South Korea's unification ministry and China's Xinhua news agency. He met Wang Huning, a Standing Committee member of the Communist Party, toured a car factory and said North Korea 'stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation'. Wang accompanied him back to the bridge.

The Guardian notes the timing: the visit falls just before the 25 October anniversary of China's first major victory in the Korean War, days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu in October 1950. Japan's Kyodo agency reported traffic controls around the bridge and a nearby war museum, plus restrictions on hotel bookings. It is Kim's first visit to China in more than a year, and comes as inter-Korean relations deteriorate — the Guardian reported this week that the North is preparing to restart propaganda loudspeakers aimed at the South.
sections.whyItMatters: Pyongyang has opened bridges toward both Moscow and Beijing, and this trip is a visible choice of weight on the Chinese side ahead of a symbolic war anniversary. For Washington and Seoul, it removes any near-term hope of splitting North Korea from China on denuclearisation.

sections.heading: Musk Confirms He Throttled Starlink, and Kyiv Pays the Price at the Front
sections.body:
Elon Musk said on Saturday that SpaceX throttled Starlink service in Ukraine, ending more than a week of confusion over who ordered the restrictions. 'Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,' he wrote on X, adding that Ukraine's military 'violated Starlink terms of service'. He said the loophole was closed last week and that Starshield — the military-tier system — is owned by the US government, with restrictions decided by the US military and ultimately by the president.

Zelenskyy said access was restored overnight and sufficient by Saturday morning, with speeds back where they need to be, improving front-line logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. He had said that while Starshield capacity was restricted, Ukraine could not track drones and missiles travelling faster than 160 km/h. Reporting conflicts on who authorised the slowdown: the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered it personally, while two US officials told CBC the order came from inside the White House. Trump said on Friday he did not know who did it and would not say if he did. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the episode showed the danger of reliance on a single provider that 'may change their view'.

Separately, CBC's investigation into the Black Sea found maritime analysts counting nearly 50 commercial vessels attacked in October alone and more than 500 attacks on merchant ships in the past year. One survivor of the HS Dignity, sunk 13 October, described a crew abandoning ship into the water and then being rammed by an unmanned surface drone as they waited for rescue.
sections.whyItMatters: A private company's terms of service now shape the tactical picture on a European battlefield, and the White House and the company disagree publicly about who pulled the lever. The Black Sea numbers show the maritime war escalating in parallel, and both push European capitals toward building alternatives they do not currently have.

sections.heading: Europe's Streets Stay Full as France Turns to Its Presidential Calendar
sections.body:
France's interior ministry put Saturday's nationwide turnout at 410,000, including 110,000 in Paris, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000, the Associated Press reported. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests. Tear gas was used in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Strasbourg and Marseille, and water cannon in Nice and Nantes, but Nunez credited 70,000 deployed officers, helicopters and armoured vehicles with preventing a repeat of the previous weekend's looting. The government's line was that 'the marches went well'.

Protests also spread in Italy, where cost-of-living demonstrations returned to the streets, and in Albania, where the government cracked down on unrest. In France the political context is the succession: Macron is in his final months, voters choose a successor in May, and the National Rally has urged protesters to convert anger into votes. In Bulgaria, voters went to the polls on Sunday in a presidential election shaped by the war next door — drone attacks on merchant shipping off the coast are estimated to have killed around two dozen seafarers, and Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the strikes' outcome 'benefits the Russian Federation' even as Sofia stopped short of blaming Moscow directly.
sections.whyItMatters: The unrest is no longer a single-issue French story but an electoral one: it feeds the National Rally ahead of the May presidential vote and is echoed in Italy and Albania. Bulgaria's vote adds a Black Sea security dimension to an otherwise ceremonial office.

sections.heading: Brazil's Coin-Toss Runoff, and a Tariff Trimmed for Maine
sections.body:
Brazil votes on Sunday in a presidential runoff between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the former president jailed for plotting a coup after the 2022 election. CBC reported that corruption and personal financial stagnation are the dominant voter concerns and that the race is a coin toss, with more than a million Lula supporters rallying in Sao Paulo on the eve of the vote according to the Guardian.

In Washington, the White House lifted tariffs on some Canadian goods — including certain packing crates and boxes — while introducing them on carpets and waste products, less than two weeks before the midterms. The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn of Canadian goods after talks collapsed in August; Carney matched it dollar for dollar last month. Maine Senator Susan Collins, in a competitive race, said she had repeatedly pressed the administration for relief on products 'crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry'. Trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said Canada stands ready to work 'constructively and in good faith'.
sections.whyItMatters: A Brazilian result either way will not settle the country's polarisation, and the size of the Lula rally suggests the runoff will be close enough to be contested. The Canadian tariff adjustment is a small but telling case of trade policy being tuned to individual Senate races weeks before an election.

bottomLine: Two of the day's most consequential decisions sit with single individuals — Trump choosing between a strike on Iran and a deal, and Tuesday's Israeli election deciding who inherits that choice. The Houthi claim to have reached Mecca and Medina's airspace, whether or not Riyadh accepts the framing, makes calm harder to restore. Meanwhile Kim Jong Un's walk across the Yalu and Musk's admission that he throttled Ukraine's battlefield connectivity both show the same pattern: alliances and dependencies are being renegotiated by the people who own the bridges and the satellites.
